content.thinking:
I'm sketching the red panda's proportions, posed balancing atop a mossy boulder with paws gathered and tail curved into an S for stability, then layering in Genshin-style cel-shading with gold filigree, tassels, and a small glowing Dendro leaf accent.

I'm thinking through the rig structure now, figuring out that the stone should be a separate root part with the panda's hip bone as a child joint, keeping a single root for the whole model.

For the stone itself, I'm planning low-poly rounded rock shapes with mossy green shading over grey-blue stone, surrounded by smaller rocks, mushrooms, ferns, and glowing dendro motifs like a leaf rune and floating motes. For the panda's coloring, I'm settling on a bright russet-orange body with a dark chestnut underbelly and legs.

I'm working out the finer features now: white face markings with reddish tear-mark lines, white-rimmed ears, a ringed tail with rust and cream bands, and black paws with pads. For proportions, I'm aiming for a slightly oversized head in that chibi Genshin style while keeping the body fairly realistic, and now I'm sketching the skeleton plan relative to the stone's flat top where the panda will stand.

I'm figuring out the body orientation facing forward, calculating hip and shoulder heights given the short legs, and settling on a balance pose with the tail raised in an S-curve, head slightly up, and all four legs spread wide on the stone's limited surface area.

For the tail, I'm going with an upward backward curl at roughly 45 degrees with a tapering bushy shape and ring pattern, deciding to keep the stone simple rather than tilted. Now I'm setting up the leg IK chains, starting with the front shoulder joint positions.

For the paws I'll skip full digit joints and instead use simple toe nubs with claw shapes attached to the final paw bone, keeping maybe one toe tip per paw to control cost while still giving separated-looking digits.

For the body itself I'm planning a spine chain from hips to chest, a short neck chain, and a head joint, with the tail as a separate chain branching off the hips, then sweeping the body profile along spine and neck with varying radius for a fluffy, belly-shifted silhouette.

Working out leg lengths next: short red panda legs, roughly 0.20 hip-to-paw, so I'm placing shoulder, elbow, and paw joints with approximate IK targets for the front limb.

For the hind leg, I'm setting the hip, knee, and ankle so the knee bends forward and the hock bends back, matching a semi-plantigrade stance, with the paw landing near the stone's surface.

Checking the hip-to-heel distance confirms the knee bends forward nicely within reach. I'm naming the four leg points so three form span joints and the last becomes the tip joint at the toe, then starting on the front legs using similar sole-based positioning from the shoulder.

I'm painting the legs dark chocolate for the stockinged look and widening the paw sweeps. For the paws, I'm deciding to add separate digit joints—maybe three toes per foot—as a cheap way to give the feet distinct, extended digits rather than a single blob foot.

Each toe becomes a single-segment chain parented to the foot, swept with a rounded radius and tipped with a light horn-colored claw spike. For the head, I'm shaping the skull as a sphere wider than it is tall, then adding cheek ruff tufts using flattened spheres or small zigzag extrusions to suggest fluffy fur tufts on the sides.

I'm separating the snout (short ellipsoid, white muzzle) and nose (black rounded triangle) from the jaw, giving the lower jaw its own joint with a small chin ellipsoid, white coloring, and interior dark mouth color -- keeping the mouth closed with just a subtle smile line rather than opening it. For the ears, I'm making them large, triangular, rounded, set high and tilted outward, with rusty red outer color and cream white fluffy inner cards, built as thick extruded outlines.

Working out ear orientation and extrusion coordinates...

I'll paint the ear surface based on normal direction: front-facing normals get the cream inner coloring with white fur texture, while the back gets rust fur, with a zigzag outline along the rim for detail.

Still shaping ear outline coordinates...

Now I'm thinking through the rest of the face details: cream inner ear with shadow gradient, white tufts along the inner edge, and then the overall red panda facial markings—white muzzle and cheek patches, white brow dots, reddish tear lines running from the eyes to the mouth, black nose and eyes, with rust fur and lighter stripes across the forehead.

For the eyes, I'm leaning anime-style with enlarged amber-green irises rather than the real animal's small dark eyes, using cel-shaded paint functions based on position relative to the head center, and deciding whether to include brow and blush details or keep them minimal to preserve the red panda look.

Now I'm working out the skull's placement in world space, setting a head joint position and defining the skull sphere, cheek ruff, and snout as scaled primitives positioned relative to that head coordinate.

Checking proportions, I'm chibifying the head a bit since real red pandas have wide heads relative to body width. For the facial fur edges I'm planning to use head-local offset coordinates to paint zigzag white patches on the cheeks, picking a rust base color with lit and shadow variants for a stylized Genshin-style palette.

Writing shared face paint function... defining the white muzzle region using distance thresholds on the local offsets so the bridge and cheeks blend continuously across head parts.

I'll implement the tear lines as a segment-distance check from eye corner to mouth corner, drawn only where the surface faces forward, and skip adding a forehead mottle detail for now since it's not essential. Then I move on to sizing the paint texture sheet at 1024 resolution.

Thinking through texel density, since the stone and panda share one paint atlas, the combined painted area (roughly 1.5 m² of stone plus 0.9 m² of panda) pushes density down to about 2mm per texel at a reasonable total painting area of 3 m², so I'll bump the paint resolution to 2048 to keep the 6mm tear lines crisp, packed into a 4096 atlas. For body coloring, I'm going with a cel-shaded countershade look: rust back, dark chestnut-black belly and legs, consistent with red panda markings.

For the fur pattern, I'm layering a fur-edge texture with rust and dark tones, nested inside a mottle variation for subtle color variegation, then wrapping the whole thing in cel shading, with the body sweep running along the default axis and a possible lighter cream-orange shoulder patch. For the tail, I'm setting up alternating rust and darker rust rings along the tail chain with a dark brown tip, considering ring period and whether to widen the bands with cream between them for a cuter, more stylized look true to red panda coloring.

Now I'm refining the ring boundaries with a small zigzag offset for texture, then working out the tail's bushy radius profile and curved path shape, raised and curling forward in an S-shape, but realizing the segment lengths add up too long compared to the body scale and need to shorten them proportionally.

I'm checking the tail's height against the model's overall proportions, then setting up the tail as a bone chain parented to the hips. Next I'm starting on the pedestal base, building a low-poly boulder shape scaled to fit beneath the figure.

Thinking about a flatter top for the boulder, I'm sketching a custom lathe profile instead of a plain sphere, with points defining a rounded shape that flattens near the top, then scaling it non-uniformly for an irregular, faceted look since lathe geometry doesn't support flat shading directly.

For the moss and surface detail, I'm planning to paint the rock using the normal's y-component plus noise so moss clusters form near the top with mottled green tones while the stone itself gets a cool grey-violet hue, all run through a cel-shading pass. I also want to add drips of moss down the sides via noise warps, small clumps or tufts along the top edges, pillow-like moss mounds with painted color variation, and fine cracks or flecks across the stone surface for texture.

For Genshin-style ornamentation, I'm thinking of giving the panda a sage-green fabric collar trimmed in gold with a round glowing medallion, plus a carved gold-rimmed dendro sigil plaque on the stone's front face and tiny glowing mushrooms nearby, possibly paired with a slender gold tail ring featuring a leaf motif for extra charm.

Adding tassels as card sprites hung facing upward, then planning the surrounding stone scene with ferns, grass tufts, and small mushrooms.

Sketching out the scale: keeping the stone around 0.7 wide with the tail reaching back to z=-0.55, and scattering ground clutter within a half-meter radius. I'm also considering a flat mossy turf base with a grass disc around radius 0.6 to tie the scene together with pebbles and ferns.

Now for the face details — adding thin white whisker sweeps, three per side, plus eyes and brows, and deciding whether tiny cream fangs peeking from the lips would add to the cuteness. I'm working out the jaw structure too, placing a small lower jaw ellipsoid with a dark inner mouth and pink tongue, and considering opening it slightly for a cheerful expression rather than keeping it fully closed.

For the eye placement, I'm using the skull's surface-hit function to position them symmetrically, mirrored by sign for left/right, computing the x-offset from the skull's width and a roughly 32-degree angle to land the eye sockets correctly.

I'm sizing the eyes slightly smaller than the spacing would suggest, around 0.044 by 0.06, keeping in mind red pandas have small eyes but anime style calls for bigger ones. I'm checking that the eyes sit on the rust-colored fur between the eyebrow spots and white muzzle, with the tear marks starting from the eye bottoms, then positioning the ears on the skull's top sides, rooted in with outward and forward tilts, sizing them fairly large but scaling down slightly to 0.85 for proportion.

Now I'm working out the ear outline shape as a triangular wide base with a rounded tip pointing outward, defining the extrusion frame so the ear sits correctly on the head flank with proper tilt.

For the inside coloring I'm mapping an elliptical zone near the ear's center to cream-white fur, mimicking the pale tufts real red pandas have inside their ears, while the front rim stays rust with lighter edging near the tip and the back leans toward darker chestnut near the base.

Now I'm thinking through cheek ruff tufts — small pointed cone shapes extruded outward from each cheek in white/cream to suggest fur spikes, plus a few rust-colored tufts near the crown, before moving on to how the mantle fur sweeps from neck into head.

For broader fur, I'm considering card-based tufts: flat textured billboards that read color from a paint at the root rather than per-vertex, so a grey tuft texture tinted by the coat paint keeps colors consistent. I'd apply these cards to the tail (using the ring pattern) and body edges, angled with a lean of about 70 degrees to follow the fur flow and break up the silhouette.

Thinking more about placement, I'd keep it moderate — around 150 cards concentrated at silhouette edges like tail tip, chest fringe, and cheeks, since dense cards can look too hairy for the cel style. The tricky part is that tail color depends on arc-length parameter t, but at card roots I may only have position and normal available, not that parameter directly — so I'd need to compute t by finding the closest point on the tail path at each card root instead, even though that adds per-texel cost across roughly 100k tail texels.

I'll unify the sweep and card shading by defining one shared ring-color function based on t and angle, using the cheap array lookup for the sweep and the closest-point lookup for cards, so they stay visually consistent despite the different sampling methods.

Now I'm thinking through the glowing accents — dendro motes shaped like tiny leaves or diamonds, glowing runes carved into stone, and glowing mushrooms, all rendered with flat emissive colors rather than cel shading. For the emblem, I want a carved sigil plaque on the front face of the boulder showing a leaf-in-circle dendro symbol, implemented as a glowing decal projected onto the stone surface.

I'm designing the stone perch as two stacked stones: a wider, flatter base boulder and a smaller, rounder stone balanced on top where the panda actually stands, elongated along the z-axis so the panda's stance fits comfortably, with moss detailing on the upper stone's flattened top and a raycast approach planned to determine the exact standing height.

I'll cast a ray down onto the stone surface to find the actual top height for each paw, since the panda's limbs need to be built after the stone's root joint is established so foot placement is accurate. I'm also scattering small moss tufts across the top surface away from where the paws will rest, and confirming that painted flat colors on the geometry will support the cel-shaded look I'm going for while staying within budget.

Defining the fur color palette...

Adding dendro glow and teal accents for the panda accessories, then moving to plan the body path coordinates relative to the stone's top height.

Still defining joint chains...

I'm reasoning that hips should be the root joint of the spine chain itself, parented to base, rather than a separate joint before it -- so I can define the spine chain with named joints where the first one, "hips", doubles as the chain's starting point.

Now I'm working out parenting for the rest of the skeleton: tail attaches at hips, hind legs attach at hips, front legs and neck attach at chest (the spine chain's last joint). For the body mesh, I'm considering sweeping a surface along a path that spans the full spine plus neck, possibly joining two separate sweeps rather than one combined path.

Defining body radius profile and ruff...

For the legs, I'm chaining limb points off the chest with tapering sweep radii—thicker upper legs narrowing toward wrists, with hind thighs bulkier than front, then shaping the paw at the final span.

Working out foot placement...

Setting the foot region radii for the taper, and making sure the round caps at the toe extend slightly past the target endpoint so the paw length accounts for that extra radius.

Now I'm planning the toes: three capsule-shaped sweeps per foot fanning out from the paw front, each with a small claw spike in a cream-horn color, and naming joints consistently per side for the toe structure.

I'm skipping visible paw pads since they'd be hidden underneath, keeping foot and toe colors dark with slightly lighter fingertips. For limb construction I'm planning the joint bend hints and setting the front leg root position symmetrically along the x-axis, figuring I'll debug by running it.

Setting up chain naming for shoulder, elbow, wrist, and paw joints with left/right side prefixes based on sign, then checking leg spacing fits within the stone's radius. For the tail, I'm defining a six-segment chain parented to the hips, then adding a torus-shaped gold band wrapped around the tail at an early segment, oriented along the tail's tangent direction.

Now I'm planning the neck collar — a teal torus band around the neck chain with thinner gold trim rings on each edge, plus a front medallion pendant hanging down the chest.

I'll place the pendant hanging at the chest front, connected by a chain or ribbon strands back to a collar ring around the neck base. Rather than keep calculating positions blindly, I should just build the model and use preview renders to iterate, double-checking the Builder API signatures for parts, decals, surfaces, and glow as I go.

input.command: cd ~/tmp-archive/sonnet-100/redPandaSonnet/ && sed -n 60,170p src/builder.ts; sed -n 1,60p src/ik.ts | head -80
